title: DNS: Domain Name Resolution
summary: How a hostname becomes an IP address, the DNS hierarchy of resolvers and authoritative servers, and the record types and caching behavior interviewers probe.

slides.markdown:
Computers route by IP address; humans remember names. **DNS** is the internet's phonebook — a distributed system that maps `example.com` to something like `93.184.216.34`, so nobody has to memorize numbers.

It's distributed on purpose: no single server could handle every lookup on Earth, and no single company should own the map for the entire internet. That distribution is exactly where the hierarchy in the next slides comes from.

DNS is a tree, not a flat table. At the top sit 13 logical **root servers**. Below them, **TLD servers** handle `.com`, `.org`, `.io`. Below those, **authoritative servers** hold the actual records for a domain like `example.com`.

Each level only knows where to send you *next* — root points to the `.com` TLD, that TLD points to `example.com`'s authoritative server, which alone has the real IP.

assets.alt: DNS hierarchy from root to TLD to authoritative servers

slides.markdown:
Your device doesn't walk the whole tree itself — it asks a **recursive resolver** (often your ISP's, or a public one like `8.8.8.8`) to do the legwork. The resolver walks root → TLD → authoritative on your behalf and hands back just the final answer.

The **authoritative server** for a domain is the actual source of truth for its records; the resolver is a middleman that does the walking and caches results for everyone else asking.

assets.alt: Recursive resolver querying root, TLD, and authoritative servers on behalf of a client

slides.markdown:
Looking up `www.example.com` for the first time: browser cache (empty) → OS resolver cache (empty) → recursive resolver → root server ("ask the `.com` TLD server") → TLD server ("ask `example.com`'s authoritative server") → authoritative server ("here's the IP").

Every layer checks its own cache first — that's why a *repeat* lookup for a site you visited five minutes ago is nearly instant, skipping most of this chain entirely.

assets.alt: Full DNS resolution walkthrough from browser cache to authoritative server

slides.markdown:
A handful of record types cover almost everything an interview will ask:

- **A** — hostname to IPv4 address.
- **AAAA** — hostname to IPv6 address.
- **CNAME** — an alias pointing to another hostname (not directly to an IP).
- **MX** — which mail servers handle email for a domain, with priority.
- **TXT** — free-form text, commonly used for domain verification and SPF/DKIM.
- **NS** — which name servers are authoritative for a domain.

A `CNAME` can't coexist with other records on the same name — that's a common gotcha when setting up a bare/apex domain.

In a **recursive** query, the resolver promises a final answer or an error — the client asks once and waits. In an **iterative** query, the server being asked can reply with "I don't know, but ask this other server" — a referral, not an answer.

Clients typically issue recursive queries to their resolver; the resolver then issues iterative queries up the chain (root, TLD, authoritative) on the client's behalf, following referrals until it gets a real answer.

Every DNS record ships with a **TTL (time to live)** — how long a resolver is allowed to cache it before asking again. A low TTL (like 60 seconds) means changes propagate fast but load on authoritative servers is higher; a high TTL (like a day) is efficient but slow to update.

This is why migrating a domain to a new IP isn't instant: every resolver that cached the old record honors its TTL before it re-checks, so old and new answers coexist across the internet during the transition window.

slides.sectionTitle: DNS over UDP, falling back to TCP
slides.markdown:
DNS defaults to **UDP** — a query and response usually fit in one round trip with no connection setup, which matters for a lookup that happens on every single new hostname.

It falls back to **TCP** when a response would exceed a single UDP datagram's practical size (large responses like `DNSSEC` or many records), or for zone transfers between name servers. See [UDP & Choosing TCP vs UDP](udp-and-tcp-vs-udp) for why UDP suits this pattern.

Because a domain can have **multiple A records**, a resolver can return several IPs for one hostname and rotate the order (round-robin DNS) — a crude but simple way to spread traffic across several servers without any dedicated load balancer.

It's coarse: DNS has no idea which server is healthy or overloaded right now, it just cycles through a list. See [Load Balancing — Layers & Algorithms](load-balancing-layers-algorithms) for the finer-grained alternatives.

DNS's trust model — accept whatever answer comes back, cache it, move on — is exactly what makes it attackable. **Cache poisoning** injects a forged response into a resolver's cache so it hands out a wrong (attacker-controlled) IP to everyone who asks next.

**Spoofing** forges a DNS response in transit, betting it arrives before the real one. Both exploit the same weakness: DNS over plain UDP has no built-in way to verify a response is genuinely from the authoritative server. See [Common Network Attacks](common-network-attacks).

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming DNS changes are instant
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I updated the DNS record, so everyone should see the new value right away."

**Why it's wrong:** every resolver that already cached the old record keeps serving it until its **TTL** expires — and some ISPs or corporate networks cache more aggressively than the TTL even suggests.

**Correct model:** plan migrations around TTL. Lower the TTL well *before* a planned change (giving old caches time to expire on the old, short value), make the change, then raise TTL back once you've confirmed propagation.
